rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The second person plural reading shifts the warning from the People of the Book to the Muslim community, making them the addressees of divine surveillance.
rows.anchor: 2nd person plural variant: ""what YOU do"" — shifts the warning from 3rd person

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: Some readers pause without the final yāʾ while others restore it in both words; the full form makes God's first person object explicit.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: some readers pause on dāʿ/daʿān (without yāʾ) or restore full yāʾ on both

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: The ten-reader form retains final yāʾ in both words, making the first-person object Me explicit rather than implied.
rows.anchor: Ten-reader variant: full yāʾ on both words. Makes the ""Me"" (nī) in daʿānī fully explicit

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: The variant cluster also affects daʿānī: the pausal form drops the nūn of protection, while the full form restores the first person suffix.
rows.anchor: See word 11 — same variant cluster affects daʿāni. Pausal form daʿān strips the nūn of wiqāya

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: The ten-reader form restores final yāʾ and the explicit first person object suffix Me.
rows.anchor: Ten-reader: full yāʾ restoring explicit ""Me"" suffix.

rows.speaker: Y-iḍ
rows.claim: A fatḥa on the yāʾ is grammatically valid alongside bī and adds phonetic weight to the divine self-reference.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: fatḥa on yāʾ (biya vs bī). Grammatically both valid for preposition + 1sg pronoun

rows.speaker: skn
rows.claim: Sukūn on hāʾ compresses wa-huwa to wa-hwa in rapid recitation without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on hāʾ: wa-hwa instead of wa-huwa — phonetic compression in rapid recitation; no semantic change

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: A ḍamma-kasra blend on qāf contrasts with pure kasra; both readings are canonical, and the blend preserves an archaic pronunciation without semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift on qāf: ḍamma-kasra blend (qᵘīla) vs pure kasra (qīla); ishbāʿ al-ḍamma

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: The pronoun suffix is read with either kasra or ḍamma, a dialectal phonological variant without semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Vowel change on pronoun suffix: kasra → ḍamma (hinna → hunna); dialectal phonological variant

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: The suffix again has a kasra versus ḍamma reading, representing dialectal pronunciation without a semantic change.
rows.anchor: Vowel change on pronoun suffix: kasra → ḍamma (hinna → hunna); dialectal phonological variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading uses the first person yāʾ in its basic form.
rows.anchor: Standard reading with yāʾ al-mutakallim in its basic form

rows.speaker: Y-iḍ
rows.claim: The variant places fatḥa on the final yāʾ, changing pronunciation and melody but not meaning.
rows.anchor: Variant with fatḥa on the final yāʾ (minniya) — a phonological variant in the treatment of the 1st person pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: Vr
rows.claim: Form I means Zakariyyā took charge of Mary himself, shifting agency from God's assignment to Zakariyyā's active guardianship.
rows.anchor: Form I kafala (simple): ""and he took charge of her"" — Zakariyyā is the subject who actively takes guardianship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard Form II causative reading makes God the agent who appoints Zakariyyā as Mary's guardian.
rows.anchor: Form II kaffala (causative): ""and He [God] made him [Zakariyyā] her guardian"" — standard reading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard name form is shortened, without hamza and ending in alif maqṣūra.
rows.anchor: Standard: shortened form without hamza, ending in alif maqṣūra

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The extended form adds hamza and ḍamma, with nominative case marking.
rows.anchor: Extended with hamza and ḍamma: full Arabic morphological adaptation with nominative case marking

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: The extended hamza form with fatḥa is accusative, distinguishing whether Zakariyyā is construed as subject or object of kaffala.
rows.anchor: Extended with hamza and fatḥa: case-marked accusative form — significant because it determines whether zakariyyā is subject or object of kaffala

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard form of Zakariyyā's name is shortened.
rows.anchor: Standard: shortened form

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The extended form with hamza and nominative ḍamma fits Zakariyyā's role as subject of dakhala.
rows.anchor: Extended with hamza and ḍamma: nominative, consistent with subject-of-dakhala role

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: The pronoun hāʾ has kasra in ladayhim or ḍamma in ladayhum; both are canonical dialectal forms in the seven-reader system.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift on the hāʾ: ladayhim (kasra) vs. ladayhum (ḍamma) — dialectal variation in the 3mp pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The second person plural reading changes narration about others into direct address to the audience.
rows.anchor: Second person plural (you seek) instead of third person (they seek) — shifts the address from narration about others

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The second person passive means you are returned rather than they are returned, directly addressing the audience with its inevitable return.
rows.anchor: Second person plural passive — ""you are returned"" instead of ""they are returned""; shifts to direct address

rows.speaker: Pss
rows.claim: The active third person plural means they return, presenting the subjects as choosing to return rather than being returned.
rows.anchor: Third person plural active (Form I) — ""they return"" — active voice; the subjects choose to return

rows.speaker: Y-id
rows.claim: The shortened final vowel in yadī contrasts with yadiya, a minor phonetic difference without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: shortened final vowel (yadī instead of yadiya) -- minor phonetic difference, no semantic change

rows.speaker: Y-id
rows.claim: An added fatḥa on the final yāʾ lengthens the pronunciation of innī without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: added fatḥa on final yā' (inniya instead of innī) -- phonetic lengthening variant, no semantic change

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: The nominative baynukum makes the relation itself the subject of taqaṭṭaʿa, as though the bond between them were a substantive thing that was severed.
rows.anchor: Nominative reading — baynukum becomes the subject of taqaṭṭaʿa: ""your between-ness has been severed""

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No variant is reported for this word; the standard reading is unanimous across canonical qirāʾāt.
rows.anchor: No variant reported for this word — standard reading unanimous across canonical qira'at

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: A nominative ending instead of genitive could make malāʾika the subject of a nominal sentence rather than the preposition's object, restructuring the predication.
rows.anchor: Nominative ending -u instead of genitive -i; if read as nominative, malāʾika could be subject of a nominal sentence

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: Both kasra and ḍamma on ṭāʾ are valid Form I patterns; the ḍamma may sound heavier and more forceful.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: kasra→ḍamma on ṭāʾ (yabṭishūna→yabṭushūna); both are valid Form I patterns

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: Before hamzat al-waṣl, qul may take liaison kasra or ḍamma; the latter preserves the imperative's original vowel while kasra assimilates to the liaison context.
rows.anchor: Liaison vowel variant: qul-i (kasra) vs qul-u (ḍamma) before hamzat al-waṣl of udʿū

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: The full yāʾ form explicitly restores the first person object pronoun that is otherwise implied by the nūn's kasra.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ restoration: kīdūni→kīdūnī — the 1s object pronoun yāʾ is written explicitly

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: A pausal form with sukūn alternates with the continuous form retaining full yāʾ, reflecting recitation context.
rows.anchor: Pausal vs continuous variant: kīdūn (with sukūn, pausal) alternating with kīdūnī (full yāʾ, continuous)

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: The full yāʾ explicitly restores the first person pronoun otherwise implied by the nūn's kasra.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ restoration: tunẓirūni→tunẓirūnī — explicit 1s pronoun yāʾ written rather than implied

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: Al-ghiyūb with kasra and al-ghuyūb with ḍamma are both canonical plural forms of ghayb without a semantic difference; kasra may reflect dialect.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on ghayn instead of ḍamma — al-ghiyūb vs. al-ghuyūb; both are canonical plural forms of ghayb

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: The plural ṣalawāt reading presents the Prophet's prayers as multiple invocations or an ongoing supplicatory practice.
rows.anchor: Plural form (ṣalawāt) — canonical variant among 7 readers; pluralizes the Prophet's prayers, implying multiple invocations

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: Adding yāʾ after nūn al-wiqāya extends the first person pronoun phonetically without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Addition of yāʾ after nūn al-wiqāya — phonetic extension of the 1s pronoun; no semantic change

rows.speaker: Qunbul/Ruways
rows.claim: The sin reading for ṣād is attributed to Qunbul and Ruways; both forms trace to the same Semitic root for road.
rows.anchor: sin replaces ṣād — Qunbul/Ruways reading; both ṣirāṭ and sirāṭ trace t

rows.speaker: Khalaf ʿan Ḥamza
rows.claim: Khalaf from Ḥamza uses ishmām, coloring ṣād slightly with zāy to produce an intermediate sound between ṣ and s.
rows.anchor: ishmām: ṣād pronounced with a slight zāy coloring — Khalaf ʿan Ḥamza; a phonetic intermediate between ṣ and s

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: Tanwīn treats Thamūd as triptote and a masculine Arabic noun rather than a diptote foreign or tribal proper name.
rows.anchor: Tanwīn added (ثَمُودًا vs ثَمُودَ) — treating the name as fully declinable (triptote/munṣarif) rather than diptote

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: Genitive tanwīn treats Thamūd as fully declinable and suggests an Arabic-origin noun rather than a foreign proper name.
rows.anchor: Genitive tanwīn (li-Thamūdin vs li-Thamūda) — treating the name as triptote/fully declinable

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: The genitive agrees in case with ilāhin, making ghayr a direct adjective meaning a god other than Him.
rows.anchor: Genitive — agrees with ilāhin in case, making ghayr a direct adjective of the indefinite noun

rows.speaker: Y-iḍ
rows.claim: Fatḥa is added to the final yāʾ as an alternate pronunciation of the first person suffix, with no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Addition of fatḥa on final yāʾ — phonological variant with no semantic change, alternate realization of 1s pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: Y-iḍ
rows.claim: The same fatḥa on final yāʾ appears in wa-innī, a phonological variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Addition of fatḥa on final yāʾ in the wa-innī compound — phonological variant matching the pattern of word 22

rows.speaker: Lvw|pl
rows.claim: The plural reading makes the mockery sharper by implying Shuaib's many prayers are what interfere and command them.
rows.anchor: Plural ṣalawāt: ""do your prayers (multiple) command you"" — pluralizing intensifies the mockery

rows.speaker: Imp
rows.claim: The second person tūqidūna makes the listeners themselves the metalworkers, personalizing the parable instead of speaking of them in third person.
rows.anchor: 2mp tūqidūna (you kindle) vs. 3mp yūqidūna (they kindle) — shifts addressee

rows.speaker: vhr
rows.claim: Kasra on nūn is explained by two adjacent quiescent letters; ḍamma follows the preceding nāʾ or the vowel in ʿibāda.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: kasra on nūn (an-i) → ḍamma (an-u); both canonical among the Seven. The kasra is due to the meeting of two sākinas

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: One plural-stem pronunciation changes hamza from ḍamma to kasra and mīm from fatḥa to kasra, a dialectal vowel variant.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: ḍamma to kasra on hamza (u→i), and fatha to kasra on mīm — dialectal variation

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: An intermediate form changes only hamza from ḍamma to kasra while mīm retains fatḥa.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift: ḍamma to kasra on hamza only (u→i), mīm retains fatḥa — intermediate variant

rows.speaker: Y-iḍ
rows.claim: The final yāʾ in inniya is pronounced with fatḥa, an alternative canonical pronunciation without change in meaning.
rows.anchor: Final yāʾ pronounced with fatḥa — an alternative canonical reading that adds phonetic openness to the pronoun ending

rows.speaker: ḥf
rows.claim: Reading anna rather than inna makes the clause subordinate, meaning that I am your Lord, with an elided main clause such as Know.
rows.anchor: Hamza changed from kasra to fatḥa: shifts from inna (emphatic particle) to anna (complementizer ""that"")

rows.speaker: Yz
rows.claim: The ten-reader form restores final yāʾ to wādī, while the shortened form follows standard rasm; the difference has no semantic effect.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ restored (bi-l-wādī) vs shortened form (bi-l-wādi) — the 10-reader variant restores the final yāʾ

rows.speaker: Tnw
rows.claim: Without tanwīn, Ṭuwā is treated as a diptote proper name, foreign or feminine, that rejects nunation.
rows.anchor: Without tanwīn: read as diptote proper noun (mamūʿ min al-ṣarf) — the name Ṭuwā is treated as a definite foreign or feminine proper noun

rows.speaker: Gm
rows.claim: Reading anna makes the clause subordinate to the preceding verb, meaning and that I chose you.
rows.anchor: Reading with anna (intensifying particle + first-person) instead of ana (pronoun): changes syntactic structure

rows.speaker: Pf|Dot
rows.claim: The variant uses the first person plural We have chosen instead of singular I chose, shifting from intimate singular address to majestic divine plural.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with 1st person plural -nā instead of singular -tu: ""We have chosen you"" — majestic plural vs singular divine ""I""

rows.speaker: HzT
rows.claim: The variant handles the hamza between rāʾ and yāʾ differently while preserving the full syllabic length of Isrāʾīl.
rows.anchor: Hamza-treatment variant — alternative handling of the hamza between rāʾ and yāʾ, preserving full syllabic length

rows.speaker: Vr
rows.claim: Form V adds an intensive reflexive sense: the object eagerly snatches up or greedily devours the magicians' work of its own accord.
rows.anchor: instead of Form I — adds reflexive-intensive meaning

rows.speaker: CE
rows.claim: An indicative ending in rafʿ makes it an independent statement that it swallows, rather than a jussive consequence of the imperative.
rows.anchor: Form V with indicative -u ending (rafʿ) rather than jussive — reads as independent statement ""it swallows up""

rows.speaker: Assim
rows.claim: Assimilation of the first tāʾ into the second produces the heavy cluster, which the source says enacts the physical struggle of swallowing.
rows.anchor: Assimilated tāʾ: original tatalaqqaf with first tāʾ assimilated into second — Form VI or assimilated Form V

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: The verbal noun siḥr shifts the sense from a sorcerer's trick to sorcery as the act or craft itself, making the craft the scheming agent.
rows.anchor: verbal noun) instead of sāḥirin (active participle)

rows.speaker: Ḥamza and others
rows.claim: An explicit interrogative hamza turns the declaration into Pharaoh's incredulous question and makes his outrage directly rhetorical.
rows.anchor: Interrogative hamza prefix — transforms declarative ""you believed"" into incredulous question ""did you believe?""

rows.speaker: hmz
rows.claim: The second hamza is softened through tashīl, creating a smoother transition while retaining the interrogative force.
rows.anchor: Variant hamza realization — different orthographic/phonetic treatment of the interrogative hamza; tashīl (softening) of second hamza

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: Kasra rather than fatḥa on mīm makes the genitive inflection explicit in the construct form.
rows.anchor: Kasra on mīm instead of fatḥa — genitive inflection explicit; standard construct reading in many qira'at

rows.speaker: Y-iḍ
rows.claim: The variant adds yāʾ with iḍāfa, explicitly marking possession in the pronoun suffix.
rows.anchor: Added yāʾ with iḍāfa — explicit possessive marker; canonical variant extending the pronoun suffix

rows.speaker: HzT
rows.claim: This ten-reader form varies the orthographic handling of the hamza-alif sequence in Isrāʾīl.
rows.anchor: Variant hamza treatment — different orthographic handling of the hamza-alif sequence; in 10-reader canon

rows.speaker: skn
rows.claim: Fatḥa rather than sukūn on hāʾ changes syllable weight in zahara versus zahra without affecting the root meaning.
rows.anchor: Fatḥa on hāʾ instead of sukūn — zaharata vs. zahrata; morphological variant affecting syllable weight

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: Form III difāʿ suggests sustained or reciprocal defense, while Form I dafʿ can indicate a single act of pushing.
rows.anchor: difāʿ (Form III verbal noun) vs. dafʿ (Form I) — difāʿ implies sustained/reciprocal defense; dafʿ implies single-act pushing

rows.speaker: Vr
rows.claim: Form I passive indicates simple demolition, whereas standard Form II suggests thorough or repeated destruction.
rows.anchor: Form I passive hudimat (simple demolition) vs. standard Form II huddimat (intensive demolition) — both canonical

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: Kasra on sīn yields mansikan, an alternative canonical form of the noun of place or time.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on sīn instead of fatḥa — mansikan as alternative form of the noun of place/time

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: The singular ʿaẓman treats bone as substance or material, while plural ʿiẓāman presents the bones as a system.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: singular ʿaẓman instead of plural ʿiẓāman — shifts from ""bones"" (system) to ""bone"" (substance/material)

rows.speaker: Lvw
rows.claim: Singular al-ʿaẓma describes bone as substance rather than plural al-ʿiẓāma as a system of bones.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: singular al-ʿaẓma instead of plural al-ʿiẓāma — ""the bone"" as substance rather than ""the bones"" as system

rows.speaker: vw
rows.claim: Kasra rather than ḍamma on bāʾ is an attested dialectal pronunciation of the broken plural without semantic effect.
rows.anchor: Vowel variant: kasra on bāʾ instead of ḍamma — dialectal pronunciation of the broken plural, no semantic impact
